notes.h: Why textiles matter in the home
notes.b: A textile is a material made from fibres or yarns (the threads spun from fibres) that has been woven, knitted or otherwise made into fabric. Textiles are a household resource, like food or fuel: they are bought, used, cared for and eventually replaced.
points: Textiles serve household purposes, such as bedding, curtains, carpets, towels and upholstery, and clothing purposes.
Because textiles cost money and need care, choosing well saves money and effort over the life of the item.
Most household textiles do several jobs at once. A curtain, for example, gives privacy, decoration and some warmth.
notes.tip: Examiners like an example item with every function or property you give, so name a real household item each time.

notes.b: Textiles are used throughout the home for practical and decorative purposes, often several at once. Examiners often ask for a list of functions, so learn each one with its example item.
points: Warmth and insulation: blankets, duvets, throws and thick curtains trap still air within their fibres and layers, reducing heat loss from the body.
Sound absorption (sound insulation): carpets, rugs, curtains and upholstery absorb sound and reduce echo in a room.
Privacy and light control: curtains, net curtains and blinds screen the room from view and control the light entering it.
Comfort: cushions, mattress covers, bed linen and upholstery give softness and support.
Protection: oven gloves and aprons protect the user from heat and spills, carpets protect floors from wear, and mattress protectors protect the mattress.
Absorbency: towels, tea towels, dishcloths and bath mats take up water from the body, from dishes or from the floor, which makes washing and drying easier.
Decoration and aesthetics: curtains, cushions, wall hangings, bedspreads and rugs add colour, pattern and texture to a room.
Hygiene: washable textiles can be laundered to remove dirt and micro-organisms. Safety is a further function, because fire-resistant finishes make textiles safer.
notes.tip: When asked to outline three or four functions, give each function with an example item, such as carpets for insulation, cushions for comfort, oven gloves for protection, rugs for sound absorption, towels for absorbency, blinds for privacy, blankets for warmth and curtains for decoration.

notes.b: A textile is chosen by weighing the properties of the fabric against the job it has to do, the money available and the household's preferences. Examiners often ask for three or four of these criteria, each with an explanation.
points: Fitness for purpose: the fabric's properties must suit its job, for example a towel needs absorbency and a curtain needs to drape well and resist fading.

Suitability in use: the fabric must withstand the wear, washing and conditions of the room it is used in, such as a kitchen, a living room or a child's bedroom. Purpose is the job; use is the wear and conditions, and both come under fitness.
Cost: the price must fit the budget and the expected life of the item, so a durable fabric can be better value. Wool and silk cost more than most other fibres.
Personal choice: likes and dislikes, colour and style, comfort, a preference for natural or easy-care synthetic fabrics, and current trends.
Aesthetic appeal: appearance, drape, weight, texture, lustre, colour and pattern, because the textile must look right in the room.
Care and cleaning: whether the fabric is washable or dry clean, how much ironing it needs, and its fade resistance, stain resistance and shrinkage, which affect how practical it is for the household.
Safety: a flame-retardant finish or fire-resistance label is wanted, and a loose or pile surface is avoided because it burns more easily.

In a longer Higher Level answer, durability (how long the fabric lasts), finishes (treatments added to improve a fabric) and sustainability (the environmental effect of the fabric) are also accepted, with one developed line on each.
notes.tip: For a 12-mark Higher answer, develop points on cost, properties, aesthetics, care, safety, trends, durability and sustainability. Do not say that natural fibres cost more than synthetic ones, because cotton and linen are not dear; say wool and silk.

notes.h: Fabric properties that matter in the home
notes.b: Each property below describes how a fabric behaves in use. Define each in plain words and give an example fabric, since examiners ask what a property means and which fabric has it.
points: Absorbent: the fabric takes in and holds moisture. Cotton and linen are absorbent, which makes them suitable for towels, and an absorbent fabric also takes up dye easily.
Flammable: the fabric ignites and burns readily when exposed to a flame, creating a fire risk. Cotton burns easily, so flammability is not wanted in household textiles.

Crease-resistant: the fabric resists wrinkling in wear and washing and returns towards its smooth shape, so less ironing is needed. Polyester and wool resist creasing, but cotton and linen crease unless finished.
Colourfast: the colour resists running in water and fading in light, so it stays bright after washing, because the dye is fixed firmly to the fibres.
Durable (hard wearing): the fabric resists abrasion, tearing and wear over a long period of use.
Drape: the way a fabric hangs in folds. A good drape suits curtains and loose clothing.
Other properties examiners accept as desirable are warm, strong, washable, easy to dye, shrink resistant, stain resistant, quick drying and resilient (springs back into shape).
Static: synthetic fibres build up static electricity, so the fabric clings, and fabric conditioner reduces this. Wool can shrink in hot washing.
notes.tip: Absorbency is about moisture only, so never use it to mean warm. Flammable and inflammable mean the same, so use flammable. Irritant, flammable and windproof are not properties you want in household textiles, so do not tick them when asked which are desirable.

notes.b: Choosing a fabric means matching its properties to the job of the item. When you recommend a fabric for a stated item, give the fabric and a reason from its properties.
points: Cotton towels: absorbent, strong when wet and able to withstand hot washing.
Linen tea towels: absorbent, strong and quick drying, but they crease easily unless treated.
Polyester curtains: drape well, resist fading, wash easily, dry quickly and resist creasing.
Cotton curtains: easy to launder and dye, with a crisp appearance and strong when wet, but they shrink if not pre-shrunk.
Wool blankets: warm, insulating, absorbent and elastic (resilient), but they can shrink and felt (the fibres mat together) if washed at high temperatures or carelessly.
Carpets in nylon or wool: strong, hard wearing and resistant to abrasion from foot traffic.
Bed linen in cotton or polyester-cotton: washable, strong and easy to iron.
notes.tip: If asked to suggest two fabrics for living room curtains, name two (such as polyester and cotton) and give a property of each as the reason.

keyTerms.definition: The principle that a textile's properties must match the job it is required to do in the home.
The ability of a fabric to take in and hold moisture.
The tendency of a fabric to ignite and burn readily when exposed to a flame.
The ability of a fabric to resist wrinkling and recover its smooth shape during use and washing.
The ability of a fabric's colour to resist running in water and fading in light.
The way a fabric hangs and falls in folds under its own weight.
The ability of a fabric to withstand wear, abrasion and tearing over a long period of use.
The visual and tactile qualities of a textile, such as colour, pattern, texture and lustre, that make it attractive.

factCards.definition: Warmth and insulation, protection, privacy and decoration.

factCards.term: Three factors in selecting textiles for the home
factCards.definition: Fitness for purpose, cost and personal choice.

factCards.term: Fabric for towels and the reason
factCards.definition: Cotton: it is absorbent, strong when wet and easy to launder.

factCards.term: Fabric chosen for curtains and its main properties
factCards.definition: Polyester: it drapes well, is fade resistant, washes easily and resists creasing.

factCards.term: Property of untreated fabric that creates a fire risk
factCards.definition: Flammability: an untreated fabric ignites and burns readily when exposed to a flame.

factCards.term: Two natural fabrics suitable for household textiles
factCards.definition: Cotton and linen: both are absorbent and washable.

questions.prompt: Identify three functions of textiles used in a living room and give one example of a textile for each function.
questions.model: Any three of: warmth or insulation (a wool throw or rug); sound absorption (a carpet or heavy curtains); privacy (lined curtains or blinds); comfort (cushions or upholstered sofa); decoration (wall hangings or a patterned curtain); protection (a rug protecting the floor from wear).

questions.prompt: Explain how cost, fitness for purpose and personal choice influence a household's choice of textiles. Give an example for each factor.
questions.model: Fitness for purpose: a textile's properties must match its use, e.g. a towel must be absorbent and strong when wet, so cotton is chosen; a curtain must drape well and resist fading, so polyester is chosen. Cost: natural fibres such as wool and silk are more expensive than most synthetic fibres, so a family with a limited budget may choose a cheaper polyester or cotton blend for everyday items. Personal choice: preferences for colour, style, comfort and easy-care fabrics affect the choice, e.g. a household that wants low maintenance chooses a crease-resistant synthetic blend for bed linen. The factors often pull against each other, e.g. a cheap fabric may not have the properties the purpose requires, so the household must weigh cost against fitness for purpose.
